title: Decidability of conjunctive-query entailment in SROIQ
area: Database theory and finite model theory
formal:
Is Boolean conjunctive-query entailment for classical SROIQ decidable under semantics allowing both finite and infinite models? Precisely, does there exist one deterministic Turing machine \(D\) such that for every finite legal SROIQ knowledge base \(K\) and every Boolean conjunctive query \(q\), in the syntax and semantics below, \(D(K,q)\) halts with a bit satisfying
\[D(K,q)=1\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad K\models q?\]
Both \(K\) and \(q\) are input. Query atoms may use non-simple roles, including roles made transitive or affected by legal role chains. There is no bound on the size of models and no finite-model, named-witness, Horn or simple-query-role restriction. No running-time bound is requested beyond termination on every legal pair.
definitions:
Names and role expressions. Use disjoint countable sets of ordinary concept names \(A\), nominal concept names \(o\), individual names \(a\), ordinary role names \(r\), and query variables \(x\), each effectively indexed by natural numbers. There is also a distinguished universal role \(U\). A role expression is \(r\), \(r^{-}\), or \(U\). The operation \(\operatorname{Inv}\) swaps \(r\) and \(r^{-}\) and fixes \(U\). Only finitely many names occur in an input. Nominal concepts and individual names are different syntactic sorts; a nominal will denote a singleton, while an individual denotes an element. They can be linked by an assertion \(o(a)\). There are no datatypes, datatype predicates or additional rule language.

Role hierarchies and regularity. The knowledge base includes a finite role hierarchy \(\mathcal H\) of inclusions \(R_1\cdots R_\ell\sqsubseteq r\), with \(\ell\ge1\), every \(R_i\ne U\), and \(r\) an ordinary role name. We use the normalized syntax of classical SROIQ: an inverse on the right can be removed by inverting both sides and reversing the left-hand string. Trivial self-inclusions are omitted; aliases connected by cycles of ordinary role equivalences can first be identified consistently throughout the knowledge base and query. The formal input domain here consists of the normalized inclusions satisfying the following finite regularity test.

There must exist an irreflexive transitive relation \(\prec\) on the occurring non-universal role expressions and their inverses such that \(S\prec R\) if and only if \(\operatorname{Inv}(S)\prec R\). Every inclusion \(w\sqsubseteq r\) must have one of the forms
\[w=rr,\qquad w=r^{-},\qquad w=S_1\cdots S_t,\qquad w=rS_1\cdots S_t,\qquad w=S_1\cdots S_t r,\]
where, in the last three cases, \(t\ge1\) and \(S_i\prec r\) for every \(i\). The same order must work for the whole hierarchy. It need not be supplied with the input. This excludes arbitrary mutually recursive role-chain rules. Transitivity and symmetry of a role name can be written as \(rr\sqsubseteq r\) and \(r^{-}\sqsubseteq r\), respectively.

Simple roles and role assertions. Declare a role non-simple if it belongs to the least set \(\mathcal N\) satisfying these closure rules: the right-hand role of every inclusion whose left side has length at least two lies in \(\mathcal N\); \(R\in\mathcal N\) implies \(\operatorname{Inv}(R)\in\mathcal N\); and an ordinary single-role inclusion \(R\sqsubseteq S\) propagates membership from \(R\) to \(S\). For the last rule also include the inverse inclusion \(\operatorname{Inv}(R)\sqsubseteq\operatorname{Inv}(S)\) for each single-role inclusion. Every other role is simple. In the selected 2006 syntax, \(U\) is absent from role hierarchies and is simple; number restrictions on \(U\) are allowed and count all elements of the qualified concept. This makes the original universal-role convention explicit, rather than substituting the separate OWL2 syntax restrictions.

Besides \(\mathcal H\), the role box may contain \(\operatorname{Ref}(R)\), \(\operatorname{Irr}(S)\), \(\operatorname{Asy}(S)\), and \(\operatorname{Dis}(S,T)\). Here \(R,S,T\ne U\), and \(S,T\) must be simple, while the reflexive role \(R\) need not be simple. Asymmetry is strict: an edge forbids its reverse, even on the diagonal.

Concepts and the rest of the knowledge base. Concepts are the finite expressions generated by
\[C::=A\mid o\mid\top\mid\bot\mid\neg C\mid(C\sqcap C)\mid(C\sqcup C)\mid\exists R.C\mid\forall R.C\mid(\ge h\,S.C)\mid(\le h\,S.C)\mid\exists S.\mathsf{Self}.\]
The role \(R\) is arbitrary, \(S\) must be simple, and \(h\) is any nonnegative integer written in binary. A finite knowledge base \(K\) consists of the legal role box, a finite TBox of inclusions \(C\sqsubseteq E\), and a finite ABox of assertions \(C(a)\), \(R(a,b)\), \(\neg R(a,b)\), or \(a\ne b\). Positive and negative role assertions may use non-simple roles. In particular, number restrictions, self restrictions and role-property assertions have the simplicity restrictions just stated, but ordinary ABox role assertions do not acquire an extra simplicity restriction.

Interpretations. An interpretation \(\mathcal I\) has a nonempty set \(\Delta^{\mathcal I}\), finite or infinite. Each ordinary concept denotes a subset, each nominal denotes a singleton subset, each individual name denotes an element, and each ordinary role denotes a binary relation on this domain. Different names need not denote different elements or sets. Set \(U^{\mathcal I}=\Delta^{\mathcal I}\times\Delta^{\mathcal I}\) and \((r^{-})^{\mathcal I}=\{(y,x):(x,y)\in r^{\mathcal I}\}\). The relation for a string \(R_1\cdots R_\ell\) contains \((d_0,d_\ell)\) exactly when there exist intermediate elements \(d_1,\ldots,d_{\ell-1}\) with \((d_{i-1},d_i)\in R_i^{\mathcal I}\) for all \(i\).

Interpret \(\top\) as the whole domain, \(\bot\) as the empty set, negation as complement in the domain, and \(\sqcap,\sqcup\) as intersection and union. An element belongs to \((\exists R.C)^{\mathcal I}\) if it has an \(R\)-successor in \(C^{\mathcal I}\), and to \((\forall R.C)^{\mathcal I}\) if all its \(R\)-successors are in \(C^{\mathcal I}\). It belongs to \((\ge h\,S.C)^{\mathcal I}\) if at least \(h\) distinct \(S\)-successors lie in \(C^{\mathcal I}\), and to \((\le h\,S.C)^{\mathcal I}\) if there are no \(h+1\) distinct such successors. These definitions also apply to infinite successor sets. Finally \((\exists S.\mathsf{Self})^{\mathcal I}=\{d:(d,d)\in S^{\mathcal I}\}\).

A hierarchy inclusion requires inclusion of the corresponding binary relations. Reflexivity means that every \((d,d)\) belongs to the role relation; irreflexivity means that no such pair belongs; asymmetry means that \((d,e)\) in the relation excludes \((e,d)\); disjointness means the two role relations have empty intersection. A TBox inclusion requires \(C^{\mathcal I}\subseteq E^{\mathcal I}\). An ABox concept assertion requires membership of \(a^{\mathcal I}\), a positive or negative role assertion requires membership or nonmembership of \((a^{\mathcal I},b^{\mathcal I})\), and inequality requires \(a^{\mathcal I}\ne b^{\mathcal I}\). A model of \(K\) satisfies every one of its axioms and assertions.

Queries and entailment. A Boolean conjunctive query is a finite formula
\[q=\exists x_1\cdots\exists x_t\ \bigwedge_{j=1}^{b}\alpha_j,\qquad t,b\ge0,\]
whose terms are the displayed variables or individual names. Each atom is \(A(v)\), \(o(v)\), or \(r(v,w)\), allowing also the role name \(U\). All variables occurring in atoms are bound. Ordinary query role names may be simple or non-simple. Query symbols need not occur in \(K\); their interpretation still obeys the name conventions above. No query negation, inequality, equality atom, disjunction, counting, self operator or regular-path operator is included. Repeated terms are allowed, so \(r(x,x)\) is allowed without being the concept constructor \(\exists r.\mathsf{Self}\). Query assignments map variables to arbitrary domain elements, may identify different variables and may use unnamed elements. The same assignment must make every atom true; individual terms keep their interpretations. The empty conjunction is true. Write \(\mathcal I\models q\) when such an assignment exists, and \(K\models q\) when every model of \(K\) satisfies it. If \(K\) has no models, it entails every query.

Effective decision problem. Encode the finite sets of axioms and query as fully parenthesized prefix expressions, with fixed distinct tags for the constructors and name sorts, binary indices for names, and binary counts for number restrictions, separated by delimiters. Lists of expressions are delimited as finite lists. This is a finite-string representation with effective parsing; replacing it by another computably equivalent explicit encoding does not change decidability. The finite syntax, simplicity and regularity conditions are part of legal input, and can be checked effectively. The requested machine has one finite program, no oracle or nonuniform advice, and must halt with the correct bit on every legal pair. No bound on its time, space or intermediate objects is prescribed; behavior on malformed pairs is irrelevant.
answer_criterion: Provide a complete, mathematically correct Lean-checked proof that one such total decision procedure exists, or a proof of its logical negation. For a positive answer, establish soundness, completeness and termination on every finite legal pair in the full language, including arbitrary non-simple query predicates and knowledge bases whose only models are infinite. For a negative answer, establish that every deterministic Turing machine fails on some legal pair by not halting with a bit or by returning the wrong entailment answer. Undecidability only for finite-model semantics or for a stronger query or axiom language does not settle this target. Likewise, a terminating method only for Horn knowledge bases, simple-role queries, satisfiable instances with a finite model bound, or other proper restrictions is insufficient. Empirical termination of a reasoner is not a universal termination proof.
why: A basic decidability boundary for querying expressive ontologies: the logic has decidable consistency, but unrestricted conjunctive-query entailment still lacks a general resolution.

importance.reason: A longstanding foundational question connecting description logics, database queries and infinite-model reasoning, with sharply different outcomes for nearby restrictions.

progress.text: Horrocks–Kutz–Sattler define SROIQ and prove decidability of its standard consistency reasoning tasks.
Rudolph–Glimm establish query decidability with nominals, inverses and counting, including SROIQ queries restricted to simple roles.
Ortiz–Rudolph–Šimkus establish decidable path-query answering for Horn-SROIQ.
Rudolph proves finite-model conjunctive-query entailment undecidable in a SROIQ fragment; this uses finite semantics.
Steigmiller–Glimm present absorption-based checking, while explicitly retaining the full decidability question and a termination condition involving new nominals.
The revised full version of the AAAI 2026 paper proves 2ExpTime-completeness for S, including Boolean-query hardness with two transitive roles.

status_note: Checked through16 September2026. No general decision procedure or all-model undecidability proof for the specified Boolean-CQ problem was found in the bounded primary-source review. The May2026 theorem concerns S; the other checked results concern simple query roles, Horn knowledge bases, finite-model semantics or conditional termination of a practical reasoner. The distinction from the selected full classical SROIQ target is explicit.

context_blocks.text: A knowledge base describes incomplete information about a world. Its assertions name some objects, while its general axioms can require additional unnamed objects in every possible world. A Boolean query asks whether a finite relational pattern must exist. The problem is to decide whether the pattern follows from the whole specification, rather than whether it can be found among explicitly stored facts.

For example, let the knowledge base assert \(\mathsf{Person}(a)\) and \(\mathsf{Person}\sqsubseteq\exists\mathsf{knows}.\mathsf{Person}\). Every model then satisfies \(\exists x\exists y\,(\mathsf{Person}(x)\land\mathsf{knows}(x,y)\land\mathsf{Person}(y))\). No named witness for \(y\) is required. The same domain element may serve as both variables if the model permits it. A query that reuses variables across several atoms requires one common assignment satisfying all those atoms.

SROIQ combines concept negation, existential and universal restrictions, singleton concepts, inverse roles, counting and regular role chains. This expressive combination underlies the logical core of OWL 2 DL. The role restrictions in the definitions are substantive: removing regularity or allowing arbitrary counting over composite roles produces different logics. The original SROIQ paper supplies a decision procedure for consistency, but that alone does not answer arbitrary conjunctive queries.

The conjunction of K with \(\neg q\) is inconsistent exactly when K entails q, but the negation of an arbitrary joined relational pattern need not be expressible as a SROIQ knowledge base. Likewise, a finite graph built by a consistency tableau is usually a compact representation of models, not an ordinary database on which evaluating q automatically gives the right answer. Unfolding repeated nodes can change whether a query cycle exists.

Rudolph and Glimm resolved a major part of the surrounding question in 2010. They handle nominals, inverse roles and counting together, and obtain decidability for SROIQ when all binary query predicates are simple roles. Thus the mere presence of those three constructors is not the remaining obstacle. The full question on this card also allows the query to inspect roles affected by transitivity and more general role compositions.

A different positive frontier comes from Horn restrictions. Ortiz, Rudolph and Šimkus show decidability even for a stronger path-query language over Horn-SROIQ, with doubly exponential combined complexity. Horn knowledge bases exclude forms of disjunctive choice that full SROIQ permits. Their result is therefore highly relevant progress, while leaving the unrestricted combination of knowledge-base features and query joins unresolved.

The distinction between all models and finite models is particularly consequential. Rudolph proves undecidability of finite conjunctive-query entailment already in a fragment of SROIQ. This is not an undecidability proof for the semantics chosen here: the sets of countermodels differ, and the distinction can affect the answer even on a small example.

The finite-model distinction already appears with one simple role \(r\). Require \(\top\sqsubseteq(\ge1\,r.\top)\sqcap(\le1\,r.\top)\), \(\top\sqsubseteq(\le1\,r^{-}.\top)\), and \((\le0\,r^{-}.\top)(a)\). These axioms describe an injective total successor function with a named element outside its image. They have the natural-number successor chain as a model but have no finite model, since an injective function on a finite set is surjective. A fresh ordinary concept \(A\) can be empty on that infinite model, so \(\exists x\,A(x)\) is not entailed under the chosen semantics. It is vacuously entailed if only finite models are considered.

Steigmiller and Glimm’s 2019 absorption method addresses practical entailment checking in very expressive logics and is implemented in Konclude. Its termination argument depends on a bounded supply of newly generated nominals in the difficult feature combination. Useful empirical behavior and termination on substantial fragments do not establish a total procedure for every SROIQ input. This conditional termination is exactly why the inherited source continues to present full decidability as open.

There is relevant progress as recently as 2026, but on a different slice of the language. Ibáñez-García, Jung, Michielini and Murlak show that conjunctive-query entailment for S, which adds transitive roles to ALC, is 2ExpTime-complete; hardness already uses two transitive roles and a Boolean conjunctive query. Their May 2026 full version also treats restrictions giving smaller upper bounds. This settles a complexity question for S, not the decidability of full SROIQ.

A positive solution would establish that general finite query patterns can always be answered against this expressive ontology language in principle. A negative solution would identify a sharp gap between consistency checking and pattern entailment inside a standard logical framework. Either outcome would clarify which expressive features can be combined while retaining an algorithmic foundation for querying incomplete knowledge.

sentences: A SROIQ knowledge base describes incomplete information using concepts, individuals, relations, inverse relations, counting and restricted role chains.
A Boolean conjunctive query asks whether one finite relational pattern must occur in every model, including infinite models and witnesses that have no individual name.
The question is whether one ordinary algorithm can always decide that entailment for the complete specified language, with no running-time bound.
A complete Lean proof must establish a sound, complete and universally terminating decision procedure or prove that no such procedure exists.
The checked finite-model undecidability, simple-role and Horn decision procedures, practical reasoner and2026 S-fragment theorem do not settle this all-model SROIQ target.

source_formulation.text: The selected problem is Boolean CQ entailment for classical SROIQ under all-model semantics, using the normalized 2006 syntax, no datatypes and no unique-name assumption. Original universal-role uses in concepts and ABox assertions are retained. Non-simple roles are allowed in query atoms. Neither finite-model semantics nor OWL2-specific syntax restrictions are silently substituted.

checked_sources: Read the primary Horrocks–Kutz–Sattler2006 PDF, Definitions1–6 in both layout and raw extraction: signatures, regular order, five permitted RIA forms, inverse normalization, role alias footnote2, simplicity, role-property assertions, complete concept grammar, ABox syntax and interpretation. The ordinary universal role is allowed everywhere except role hierarchy/property assertions; Definition1 includes U among role names and the original simplicity convention permits its concept uses. No source definitions are left as a replacement for card definitions.

Corroborated the universal-role convention with the indexed primary Ortiz–Šimkus survey passage “Reasoning and Query Answering”, p.16: it explicitly says the original SROIQ syntax allows U as an ordinary role except in CRIAs and role-property axioms, and discusses number restrictions on U. Only that retrieved passage was inspected; no full survey-proof audit is claimed.

Read the full abstract and §8 conclusion of Rudolph–Glimm JAIR39 (2010),429–481. The journal conclusion explicitly states decidability for SROIQ if non-simple roles are disallowed as binary query predicates. Did not rely solely on the earlier conference abstract that only anticipated this extension; full decision-procedure proof not audited.

Read Ortiz–Rudolph–Šimkus IJCAI2011 full abstract and introduction defining the Horn scope and conjunctive two-way regular-path query language. It reports 2ExpTime combined and PTime data complexity for Horn-SROIQ; it does not cover full SROIQ disjunction.

This is not promoted to all-model undecidability. The card’s separate infinite-only example was checked directly via injectivity, surjectivity on a finite domain and the natural-number successor interpretation.

Read Steigmiller–Glimm2019 full introduction, conditional termination statement and §4 opening: the implementation may not terminate on SROIQ when query absorption propagates over new nominal nodes. Retained practical relevance without claiming a total general decider.
